title: Odd Seas
author: David Yearsley
content:
[![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/08/oddsea1-680x513.png)](https://www.counterpunch.org/2026/08/07/odd-
seas/)

![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/08/oddsea1-680x513.png)

_Playground at the Schliemann Museum, Ankershagen, Germany. Photo: David
Yearsley._

On a Sunday morning in the middle of July we left Berlin on bicycles for
Copenhagen—700 kilometers in seven days. The route is almost exclusively on
bike paths, mostly paved but also with stretches of gravel, dirt and sand. We
cycled through fields and forests, along rivers, canals, marshes, dunes and
countless lakes; over bridges; through villages, and baroque towns. We made it
out of the Müritz National Park in the German state of Mecklenburg-Vorpommern,
just before a massive wildfire closed the route there. Beyond the forests,
wheat and rapeseed fields stretched to the horizon. The collective farms of
the German Democratic Republic are now the capitalistic farms of the Federal
Republic of Germany. The land told its truths. Monoculture appears non-
ideological.

On the edge of the park, a beekeeper offered organic honey and proclaimed her
resistance to plans for wind farms: use less energy, not more, her sign
counseled.

Past a dairy with an old wooden plough displayed amongst a trio of modern
mechanized behemoths, we rounded into the village of Ankershagen built on a
rise in the flat landscape. A sign advertised a point of cultural interest:
“Heinrich-Schliemann Museum.” This attraction came as a complete surprise to
us. None in our party had read the guidebook we had in one of our saddlebags.

We dismounted and drank and soon learned that Schliemann, the excavator of
Ancient Troy, had been raised here, provided with a classical education thanks
to his father, Lutheran pastor of the village. There were more people then;
the region’s vast rural places are depopulating. Swatches of Brandenburg and
Mecklenburg-Vorpommern appear emptier of people than North Dakota.

The first thing that caught our eye in Ankershagen was not the church or the
vicarage. It was a large wooden horse bigger than a Winnebago. There was a
too-long tail behind it. On the horse’s flanks was a banner advertising The
Greek Festival beginning the next week.

Each in turn, we climbed up the ladder into the belly of the beast, crawled
through its empty insides and then shot out the other side: more like flying
excrement than fierce Agamemnon.

Another group of cyclists was having coffee at a table outside the vicarage’s
barn, now converted into a café. Otherwise, the complex was empty. The other
cyclists didn’t seem to notice us playing below, despite our age and size. No
visitors entered the museum. We heard the roar and whirl of a motor. A giant
tractor pulled through the village.

Nearby was a sandbox with faux ruins in it: a column capital here, the head of
a hero there; a giant urn rose from the pit near the remains of a once
impregnable fortress wall. Future Schliemanns of Mecklenburg-Vorpommern might
just catch archaeological fever in this remote place as they scrabbled for
fame and fragments.

At the far end of the grounds, across a large lawn presided over by a
magnificent copper beech, was a playground made up of a trireme oaring across
the land towards a couple of serpents rising from the sawdust waves, with a
helmeted Greek warrior standing alongside with spear and shield. I looked back
across the lawn to see if anyone was watching. They weren’t. I climbed into
the hold and took my place: the Colossus of Rhodes, a two-eyed Cyclops wearing
sunglasses, impressed the Achaean host.

I headed back to the horse. There were no kids in sight. Maybe the Greek
Festival would attract them.

![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/08/trojanhorseslide-680x911.png)

The museum was in the restored brick and timbered vicarage. The current
exhibition is devoted to another of Schliemann’s archaeological exploits—his
work at Mycenae on the Peloponnesian Peninsula. It was there that Agamemnon,
commander of the Greek forces, was murdered after returning from the Trojan
War by his wife, Clytemnestra.

We still had 70 kilometers to cover that day, so there was no time to visit
the museum: on to Rostock for the ferry to that corner of the Baltic, then
with the bikes across the Danish islands and on to Copenhagen three days later
against a relentless headwind. Poseidon had taken against us, maybe because we
didn’t do the Schliemann Museum.

As we rode on, I thought of the room in the New Museum back in Berlin where
there are still a few bits of the Trojan gold that Schliemann brought back
from his excavations. He called it Priam’s Treasure. In 1873 Schliemann was
apprehended in Athens after having smuggled "Priam’s Treasure" out of present-
day Turkey. He paid off the Ottoman authorities and made off with the booty.

In the New Museum in Berlin, there is a photo of Schliemann’s wife, Sophie,
wearing a fabulous headpiece and necklace taken from Troy. A replica of this
fabulous ensemble is displayed alongside in the glass case. The real treasure
is now in Russia, having been re-plundered by the Soviets in 1945.

Four days after passing through Schliemann’s Ankershagen, we dropped the bikes
at a railroad station café north of Copenhagen.

We flew through smoky European skies and then through smoky American skies to
Chicago. Still jet-lagged, we went to Christopher Nolan’s _Odyssey_ in the
Music Box Theatre, opened in 1929, on the North Side. The show was sold out.
The line began building an hour before the screening started. The staff had
made a papier-mâché Trojan Horse and placed it in the neo-Gothic lobby.

Homer’s _Odyssey_ is not full of laughs, but as the American actors with
American accents and the British actors with American accents hacked and
follied, avenged and ached, forgot and remembered, mourned and manned-up,
killed and were killed, I thought of Ankershagen—of the joy a kid could have
on those outsized ancient-modern toys for a lot less than the price of
admission to the Music Box ($21) and a lot less than to make and market the
movie, its budget pegged somewhere around $400 million.

The movie soundtrack’s creator is Ludwig Göransson, a Swede who landed on
Hollywood’s shores. This likably modest fellow (at least if his Academy Awards
speeches are an accurate barometer of his temperament) captured an Oscar (his
second) for his previous collaboration with Nolan on _Oppenheimer_. At the
director’s prompting, the composer’s _Odyssey_ score rejects the epic,
symphonic mode that is the default setting for sword-and-sandal blockbusters.

Instead, synthesized sounds that could be ancient glow and jangle, haunt and
harry. A panpipe longs for home. A lyre plucks at deferred courage or wily
derring-do. An android chorus hymns from the half-light a nearly forgotten and
fully neglected wife, son and kingdom. Gongs try to wake the audience and the
characters and to confuse them as soft sounds comfort them. Regret and
forgetfulness meander through thickets and fight the wind, are lulled by waves
and taunted by terror. Duty and ennui walk a faraway beach hand-in-hand, gray-
bearded and buffed-up Odysseus dallying with a cover-girl nymph—a South
African-born actor who also talks American.

Past the halfway point on the three-hour cinematic itinerary that dutifully
checks off the points on the bucket list printed in the back of the Homeric
guidebook, Odysseus and his few remaining men sail past the Sirens. Their
lethal song is a founding myth of music’s irresistible sensual power: its
craving strains enter from afar and invisibly penetrate the soul. The body
cannot hold out against the song. Nolan’s script makes quick and clumsy work
of Odysseus’s mad lust to hear it. The movie episode is more about the waxing
of the ears (the hero’s chest has already been waxed in his off-screen
trailer) and tying him to the mast than about any of the myth’s myriad
meanings.

But it is the score’s set piece. The soundtrack comes to the foreground, the
screams of the hero becoming the underscoring. It is time for music’s origin
story to be told, a moment that a composer can either charge into or withdraw
from.

Göransson begins with the shimmer of simulated women’s voices, sacral tones
frayed by signal interference. The ghost of an organ (a Greek invention) seeps
through the sonic ordeal. The mass tips downward as if into the watery depths
and the unconscious. A melody emerges from the Valium haze: panpipes; perhaps
a wet finger on one of Plato’s celestial orbs traces a melody. A rising minor
sixth that is a centuries-old signifier of desire arches upward then falls
back to a blunted dissonance, a half step above the drone, before rising again
to form an open, unresolved fifth—that icon not just of antiquity but of
eternity. Above Odysseus’s screams, the minimal music obsesses over its own
abstractions. Is it a revelation or a retreat, a profound exploration of music
and the psyche, or a loss of artistic nerve? Is it mythic music or merely mood
music?

After a few more stops (Seattle) and fires (Spokane), it was time to head
through the smoke, back home to Ithaca (New York).

The Finger Lakes were green. The next village up the lake is called Ulysses.
The village due west on the Allegheny Plateau from Ithaca is Mecklenburg.

It’s time for a Trojan Horse and trireme to come to the shores of Cayuga Lake.
Something new and old and fun—for the kids.
